2: title: "The Actor Model: How Erlang and Elixir Handle Millions of Users"
3: date: "2026-06-10T09:00:00.000Z"
4: description: "Most runtimes try to prevent failure with complex logic. Erlang and Elixir take the opposite approach: they assume everything will fail, and they use the Actor Model to make sure it doesn't matter."
5: ---
6: 
7: If you’ve ever wondered how WhatsApp manages to handle billions of messages with a relatively tiny engineering team, the answer is **The Actor Model**, implemented via the **BEAM virtual machine** (the engine behind Erlang and Elixir). 
8: 
9: While most modern languages (Java, Python, C++) struggle with the complexities of shared memory and locking, the BEAM treats concurrency as a first-class citizen. It doesn't have "threads" in the traditional sense; it has **Processes**. These are ultra-lightweight, isolated entities that communicate only through asynchronous message passing.
10: 
11: ### 1. The Share-Nothing Architecture
12: 
13: The biggest source of bugs in concurrent programming is **Shared Mutable State**. When two threads try to change the same variable at the same time, you get race conditions, deadlocks, and crashes. 
14: 
15: The Actor Model solves this by eliminating shared memory entirely. 
16: - Every "Actor" (or Process) has its own private heap and stack. 
17: - No process can read or write the memory of another process. 
18: - If Process A wants to tell Process B something, it must **copy** the data and send it as a message to B’s **Mailbox**.
19: 
20: Because there is no shared state, there are **no locks**. You never have to worry about a deadlock because a process never has to wait for a mutex to access its own data.
21: 
22: ### 2. Lightweight Processes and the Reduction Engine
23: 
24: A BEAM process is incredibly cheap. It starts with just **~2KB of memory**. You can spawn ten million processes on a single laptop without breaking a sweat.
25: 
26: To manage all these processes, the BEAM uses a **Preemptive Scheduler**. 
27: - **Reductions:** Instead of time-slicing based on milliseconds (which is imprecise), the VM counts "reductions" (roughly one function call = one reduction). 
28: - **Fairness:** Every process gets a budget of 2,000 reductions. Once it hits that limit, the scheduler forcibly pauses it and moves to the next process. This ensures that a single CPU-intensive process can never "starve" the rest of the system.
29: 
30: ### 3. The "Let It Crash" Philosophy
31: 
32: In most languages, a single unhandled exception can take down your entire application. Erlang and Elixir take a different path: they encourage you to **Let It Crash**.
33: 
34: Because processes are completely isolated, if one actor hits a bug and crashes, it doesn't affect any other part of the system. It just dies. 
35: - **Supervision Trees:** Processes are organized into hierarchies. A **Supervisor** process watches its children. If a child dies, the supervisor catches the signal and restarts the child in a known good state. 
36: 
37: This leads to "Nine Nines" of reliability. You don't build a system that never fails; you build a system that knows how to heal itself when it does.
38: 
39: ```text
40: ASCII Supervision Tree:
41:       [ Root Supervisor ]
42:              |
43:     +--------+--------+
44:     |                 |
45: [ DB Supervisor ]  [ Web Supervisor ]
46:     |                 |
47: [ DB Worker ]      [ Worker 1 ] [ Worker 2 ]
48: ```
49: 
50: ### 4. Location Transparency: The Distributed Actor
51: 
52: The most powerful part of the Actor Model is that it doesn't care where an actor lives. Sending a message to a process on your local machine looks exactly the same as sending a message to a process on a server in another data center.
53: 
54: This is **Location Transparency**. It allows you to build distributed systems without writing complex networking code. The BEAM handles the serialization and the TCP connections for you. You just send a message to a PID (Process ID), and the VM makes sure it gets there.
55: 
56: ### Conclusion
57: 
58: The Actor Model is a shift in mindset. It moves us from thinking about "how do I stop this thread from breaking my data" to "how do I organize these independent entities to achieve a goal." By embracing isolation, asynchronous messaging, and supervision, Erlang and Elixir have created the most resilient concurrency model in history. It’s the reason why the systems that *must* stay up—telecom switches, messaging backends, and financial clearings—are almost always built on the BEAM.

The Gatsby publish pipeline is failing due to an **unmet peer dependency for Mermaid diagram rendering**.

---

### Root Cause Analysis

#### 1. `gatsby-remark-mermaid` v5 requires `playwright`, not `puppeteer`
In [package.json](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/package.json#L21-L28), your dependencies include:
```json
"gatsby-remark-mermaid": "^5.0.0",
"puppeteer": "^25.8.0"
```
Older versions of `gatsby-remark-mermaid` (v2–v4) relied on `puppeteer`. However, `gatsby-remark-mermaid@5.0.0` was rewritten to use [`mermaid-isomorphic`](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/node_modules/mermaid-isomorphic/dist/mermaid-isomorphic.js#L1), which directly executes:
```javascript
import { chromium } from 'playwright';
```
And its declared peer dependency is **`"playwright": "1"`**, not `puppeteer`.

#### 2. Yarn v1 does not auto-install peer dependencies
In your GitHub Actions workflow ([.github/workflows/deploy.yml](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/.github/workflows/deploy.yml#L17)), the step `enriikke/gatsby-gh-pages-action@v2` detects [yarn.lock](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/yarn.lock) and runs `yarn install` (Yarn v1.22.22). 

Notice this warning in your CI log:
```text
warning " > gatsby-remark-mermaid@5.0.0" has unmet peer dependency "playwright@1".
```
Because Yarn v1 does not automatically install peer dependencies, `playwright` is never installed on the runner.

#### 3. Module load failure during Gatsby GraphQL queries
When Gatsby generates the blog posts via [`BlogPostBySlug`](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/src/templates/blog-post.js) querying `markdownRemark.html`, [`gatsby-transformer-remark`](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/gatsby-config.js#L32) invokes [`gatsby-remark-mermaid`](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/gatsby-config.js#L53). As soon as it dynamically imports `remark-mermaidjs`, Node's ESM loader tries to link `playwright` and fails:
```text
[ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find package 'playwright' imported from .../node_modules/mermaid-isomorphic/dist/mermaid-isomorphic.js
```

---

### Why this happens "sometimes"

1. **Before vs After Mermaid Support:** The pipeline only started failing after `gatsby-remark-mermaid` was added to [gatsby-config.js](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/gatsby-config.js#L53). All builds before that succeeded.
2. **Local vs CI differences:** If you run `npm install` locally (using modern npm v7+), npm automatically installs peer dependencies, so `playwright` may exist on your local machine. In CI, Yarn v1 is used due to [yarn.lock](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/yarn.lock), which skips peer dependencies.
3. **Lockfile sync inconsistency:** The runner also warned:
   ```text
   warning package-lock.json found. Your project contains lock files generated by tools other than Yarn.
   ```
   Both [package-lock.json](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/package-lock.json) and [yarn.lock](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/yarn.lock) are checked into the repository with different dependency resolutions.

---

### Recommended Solutions

Depending on how you want Mermaid diagrams handled:

#### Option A: Keep server-side Mermaid rendering with Playwright
1. Replace `puppeteer` with `playwright` in [package.json](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/package.json).
2. Ensure Playwright browser binaries / OS dependencies are installed in CI before `gatsby build` (e.g. `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium`).

#### Option B: Render Mermaid diagrams client-side (Simpler & Faster)
If you don't want headless browser overhead (Playwright/Chromium) running during Gatsby builds in GitHub Actions:
1. Remove `gatsby-remark-mermaid` and `puppeteer` from [package.json](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/package.json) and [gatsby-config.js](file:///Users/jaikumardewani/Projects/AI%20blogs/gatsby-config.js).

It transfers the item directly to the waiting reader state object and completes the consumer's task. This direct handoff avoids array enqueue and dequeue operations, saving CPU cache line invalidations.

15:        |                                  |

18:        |                                  v

9: For thirty years, database execution engines relied on the Volcano iterator model published by Goetz Graefe in 1990. The design was clean and elegant.
